summary: Gives an overview of the third version of the Internet-Standard Management Framework, known as SNMPv3, and how it builds on SNMPv1 and SNMPv2. It explains the modular design meant to let the framework evolve, and points to the documents that make it up, including their applicability.

plainLanguage.summary: Network managers use SNMP to read and change settings on routers, switches and servers. The first two versions were either insecure or never agreed on. This document is the guided tour of the third version: it explains what changed and points to the separate documents that specify each part.

questions: what is the difference between snmpv2c and snmpv3
what is the internet standard management framework
subtitle: A roadmap to the third version of the Internet management framework, and an explanation of why it replaced the first two.

tldr.problem: Network management needed a framework with strong security and administration, but SNMPv1 and the competing SNMPv2 variants either had none or had no consensus support.
tldr.mechanism: The third framework keeps the data definition language, MIB modules and protocol operations of its predecessor and adds a layered, modular set of security and administration specifications.
tldr.outcome: SNMPv3 became the single recommended framework, and SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c were reclassified as Historic; RFC 3410 is the tutorial introduction that ties the document set together.

sections.title: Purpose of This Document
sections.content:
This memo introduces the third version of the Internet-Standard Management Framework, called SNMPv3. It has several purposes: to describe how the SNMPv3 specifications relate to SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and the community-based SNMPv2 framework; to provide a roadmap to the many documents that contain the specifications; and to give a brief, readable summary of each of those documents. It replaces RFC 2570.

The document is deliberately tutorial and may occasionally oversimplify. Where it conflicts with the detailed specifications it points to, those specifications take precedence. It is a work product of the SNMPv3 Working Group of the IETF, and it uses the requirement key words as defined in BCP 14.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a map, not the territory. It explains the new version of the network management framework and tells you which document holds each part of the rules.

sections.title: Structure of the Framework
sections.content:
Any enterprise that deploys the framework has four basic components: several managed nodes, each running an SNMP entity that exposes its instrumentation remotely (traditionally called an agent); at least one SNMP entity that runs management applications (the manager); a management protocol that carries management information between those entities; and the management information itself. This basic structure is the same in SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3.

The specifications rest on a modular architecture, which is more than a protocol for moving data. It consists of a data definition language, the definitions of management information collected in the Management Information Base (MIB), a protocol definition, and security and administration. The chief reason for the modularity was to allow the framework to evolve, and the separation of a protocol-independent data definition language from a MIB-independent protocol was meant to let the protocol be replaced without redefining the management information. In practice this architecture eased the move from SNMPv1 to SNMPv2 and on to SNMPv3 rather than a move away from SNMP.

SNMPv3 builds on the same four components, incorporating some of them from the SNMPv2 framework by reference, and applies the same layering principles to the new security and administration capabilities. People familiar with the earlier frameworks will recognize most concepts, though some terminology has changed.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework has four moving parts: the language used to describe settings, the database of settings, the protocol that carries them, and the security that guards them. Keeping these parts separate is what let the framework keep evolving.

sections.title: The Earlier Frameworks
sections.content:
The original SNMPv1 framework is defined by the structure of management information, a more concise way to describe managed objects, and the protocol itself, with companion documents for the base set of management information and for event notifications, called traps. The data definition language used there is known as SMIv1. Because the original requirement was that the data definition language be protocol-independent, the language itself could not define traps; the protocol document defined a few generic ones, and a separate informational document showed how to define more. Many of these concepts carried forward into the later frameworks.

SNMPv2 added several advantages: expanded data types such as a 64-bit counter, better efficiency and performance through a get-bulk operator, confirmed event notifications called informs, richer error handling, improved row creation and deletion, and a refined data definition language. However, the SNMPv2 framework did not meet its original design goals because it lacked commercial-grade security and administration, including authentication with origin identification and message integrity, privacy, authorization and access control, and remote configuration.

Several earlier efforts had tried to add security, and their ideas fed the SNMPv2 work, but the resulting framework had no security and administration of its own. It was instead paired with several competing alternatives: community-based SNMPv2, which had the most support but no security, and two variants that had security but no consensus support. The SNMPv3 Working Group was chartered to produce one specification by converging the technical elements of those two variants.
sections.plainLanguage: The second version was better at the mechanics of management, but it never delivered the security everyone needed. Several rival attempts to add security split the community, so a working group was formed to merge the best ideas into one design.

sections.title: The SNMPv3 Specifications
sections.content:
The SNMPv3 specification is split into modules across several documents, deliberately so that any document can be revised or replaced as needs change. The documents fall into four categories: the data definition language, MIB modules, protocol operations, and security and administration. The first three are taken from SNMPv2; the fourth is new to SNMPv3.

The data definition language is SMIv2, which defines fundamental data types, an object model, and the rules for writing and revising MIB modules; it is accompanied by specifications for textual conventions, which are shorthand data types for human readers, and for conformance statements, which describe what an implementation must and does support. MIB modules contain object definitions, may define event notifications, and sometimes include compliance statements. Management information written in any version of the language can generally be used with any version of the protocol, with one exception: the Counter64 data type cannot be carried by a protocol engine that supports only SNMPv1.

Protocol operations and transport mappings are incorporated from SNMPv2. The design lets parts of the architecture evolve independently, and the mapping onto UDP is the preferred transport, so systems that use other mappings should also offer a proxy to UDP for interoperability. The security and administration work is a set of seven documents: this introduction, the architecture document, the message processing and dispatching document, the applications document, the User-based Security Model, the View-based Access Control Model, and the coexistence and transition document.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rules are broken into small documents that can each be updated on its own. Three of the four kinds of rules are inherited from the second version; only the security and administration part is genuinely new.

sections.title: Status of the Earlier Versions
sections.content:
Readers should check the current Internet Official Protocol Standards list for any document's status. The working group asked for extra text here about SMIv1, SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c. SMIv1 was promoted to full Standard in 1990 and is still a Standard, though it is not recommended. It was not declared Historic, even after SMIv2 reached full Standard, because other standards-track documents depend normatively on it and would themselves have to become Historic. For new work, SMIv2 has been the wise choice since about 1993, and the IETF now requires new MIB modules to be written in SMIv2.

SNMPv1 and the community-based SNMPv2c carry only trivial authentication based on plain-text community strings and are therefore fundamentally insecure. When the SNMPv3 security and administration specifications reached full Standard, the full Standard SNMPv1 and the experimental SNMPv2c specifications were declared Historic. The party-based SNMPv2 and its two variants were either made Historic around 1995 or were never on the standards track. Vendors and users are still expected to keep multilingual implementations that speak the old versions, and they should limit access through them as carefully as they limit unauthenticated SNMPv3 access.

Based on this reasoning, the working group recommends that the protocol and variant documents for the original and second frameworks be reclassified as Historic. Having reached a single recommended framework with security and administration, the group aimed to send a clear message that the third version is the framework of choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version and the popular second-version style are still used, but they were demoted because their passwords travel in plain text. Treat them as old, keep them locked down, and use the third version for anything that matters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because this is primarily a roadmap document, it introduces no new security considerations; the reader is referred to the relevant sections of each referenced document. The security story lives in those referenced documents. The User-based Security Model describes the two primary and two secondary threats it defends against: modification of information, masquerade, message stream modification, and disclosure of message contents.

To defend against those threats, the User-based Security Model uses MD5 and the Secure Hash Algorithm as keyed hashing algorithms. The result directly protects against data modification attacks, indirectly provides data origin authentication, and defends against masquerade. It uses loosely synchronized, monotonically increasing time indicators to defend against certain message stream modification attacks, with automatic clock synchronization that does not depend on third-party time sources. If disclosure protection is wanted, it uses the Data Encryption Standard in cipher block chaining mode, though this support is optional, largely because export and usage restrictions make cryptographic products hard to ship and use in many countries. All protocols used by that model rest on pre-placed keys; the architecture also permits public key mechanisms, but no standards-track SNMPv3 security model used them at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is only a guide, so it adds no new security rules of its own. The real security design lives in the model document, which defends against tampering, impersonation, replay and eavesdropping using shared secret keys.

items.title: Modification of information
items.text: An attacker alters data in transit.

items.title: Masquerade
items.text: An attacker assumes another user's identity.

items.title: Message stream modification
items.text: Messages are reordered, delayed or replayed.

items.title: Disclosure
items.text: Message contents are read by an eavesdropper.
